query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled, minor titanium addition (~2 at.%) into the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy will promote the in‐situ formation of fine Ti-based nanoprecipitates along grain boundaries, thereby toughening the material against cracking while preserving its large caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy exhibiting high caloric effects but poor mechanical integrity (cracking under load).
generation.intervention: Add approximately 2 atomic percent titanium into the base alloy composition during alloy synthesis.
generation.conditions: The alloy is processed under identical thermal and mechanical loading regimes as before. Measurements are envisioned under applied magnetic field, pressure, temperature variations and compressive loading conditions typical for caloric operation.
generation.structural_mediator: Fine, evenly distributed Ti-rich nanoprecipitates at grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Titanium acts as a microalloying element that forms coherent or semi-coherent precipitates during controlled cooling/annealing. These nanoprecipitates reinforce grain boundaries, impede crack propagation, and provide precipitation strengthening. Because the phase transformation responsible for the caloric response is largely maintained in the matrix, the high caloric performance is not sacrificed.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unchanged alloy, the Ti-added alloy is expected to show a significant improvement in mechanical integrity (e.g., compressive strength increased from values below 152 MPa to above 218 MPa) while retaining nearly the same magnitude of the caloric response (both in applied-field and pressure-field operation).
generation.baseline: Unmodified (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy which exhibits high caloric effects but is prone to cracking, with compressive strengths reported in related materials ranging from 48 MPa (low-melting In composites) to 218 MPa (epoxy-containing composites).
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective under the same range of applied-field intensities, pressure conditions, operating temperatures, and dynamic loading conditions as used previously. Extreme processing conditions outside the optimized annealing/cooling regime may alter precipitate formation and thus the outcomes.
generation.uncertainty: The precise atomic percentage of Ti and the resulting precipitate size/distribution need optimization. The impact on the caloric response, while predicted to be minimal, carries uncertainty until experimentally verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of samples: one set of the unmodified (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy and one set with an added 2 at.% Ti processed under identical conditions. Characterize the microstructure using electron microscopy to verify the formation of Ti-rich nanoprecipitates. Test mechanical integrity (compressive strength) and caloric response (e.g., adiabatic temperature change, phase transformation characteristics) under controlled applied-field and pressure-field conditions.
measurements: Grain boundary precipitate size and distribution (via transmission electron microscopy or scanning electron microscopy).
Quantitative caloric performance metrics (e.g., adiabatic temperature change, latent heat or field-induced phase transition parameters).
Comparison of phase transition behavior under applied magnetic field and pressure.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-added alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in mechanical integrity (e.g., compressive strength remains similar to or lower than the unmodified alloy) or if its caloric response is significantly diminished compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.
